harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.1706; supporting text Chap. 34 p.269, Chap. 60 p.432-433, Chap. 79 p.578-621
clinicalPearls: Candidiasis spans a spectrum: mucocutaneous disease (oral thrush, esophageal, vulvovaginal, intertriginous, paronychia/onycholysis) that is usually localized, versus rare systemic, life-threatening invasive disease such as candidemia and disseminated candidiasis (Chap. 60, p.432-433).

The usual causative organism is Candida albicans; these yeasts are normal saprophytic inhabitants of the gastrointestinal tract that overgrow and cause disease when host defenses are altered (Chap. 60, p.432-433).

Oral candidiasis (thrush) appears as white plaques on the tongue or buccal mucosa; angular fissured macerated lesions at the mouth corners (perleche) are seen with poorly fitting dentures and may be candidal (Chap. 60, p.432-433).

Intertriginous candidal lesions are characteristically edematous, erythematous, and scaly with scattered 'satellite pustules'; in males the penis, scrotum, and inner thighs are often involved (Chap. 60, p.432-433).
In contrast to dermatophyte infections, candidal infections are frequently painful and accompanied by a marked inflammatory response (Chap. 60, p.432-433).

Disseminated candidiasis (often due to Candida tropicalis) may present with a triad of fever, myalgias, and eruptive nodules; hematogenous cutaneous disease shows multiple raised papules with systemic signs (rash chapter, p.190; Chap. 79, p.621).
Candidemia and chronic disseminated candidiasis are recognized complications in neutropenic patients because Candida species are endogenous gastrointestinal flora (Chap. 79, p.578).

Candidemia is a recognized cause of endogenous endophthalmitis from hematogenous seeding; Roth's spots and retinal hemorrhages were illustrated in a liver transplant patient with candidemia from immunosuppression (Chap. 34, p.269).
harrison.pathophysiology: Candida species (most often C. albicans) are normal saprophytic commensals of the gastrointestinal tract and skin. They overgrow and become pathogenic when local or systemic host defenses are disrupted, e.g., by broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, diabetes mellitus, or immunosuppression. Mucocutaneous disease results from overgrowth at moist, macerated surfaces; invasive disease arises when the organism gains bloodstream access, frequently via intravascular catheters or the gut in neutropenic hosts (endogenous flora), producing candidemia and hematogenous (disseminated) seeding to organs, skin, and the eye (Chap. 60, p.432-433; Chap. 79, p.578).
additionalDifferentials: Tinea (pityriasis) versicolor due to Malassezia furfur (Chap. 60, p.432)
Lichen planus / oral leukoplakia for oral white lesions
Other invasive fungal infections in neutropenia: invasive aspergillosis and other molds (Chap. 79, p.578)
infectionMimics: Invasive aspergillosis and other molds (necrotic nodules) in immunocompromised hosts (Chap. 79, p.578; rash chapter)
Bacterial/septic endophthalmitis, including from endocarditis (Roth's spots also in leukemia, diabetes) (Chap. 34, p.269)
nonInfectiousMimics: Erythema nodosum (tender lower-extremity nodules) for nodular eruptions (rash chapter)
Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) (rash chapter)
additionalInvestigations: KOH preparation of skin/mucosal scrapings demonstrating yeast and pseudohyphae for mucocutaneous candidiasis (Chap. 60, p.433)
Blood cultures for candidemia (note insensitivity; see pitfalls) (Chap. 34, p.269; Chap. 79)
Dilated funduscopic examination to detect candidal endophthalmitis in candidemia (Chap. 34, p.269)
redFlags: Candidemia or suspected disseminated candidiasis in a neutropenic or immunosuppressed host (Chap. 79, p.578)
Visual loss, ocular pain, or floaters in a patient with candidemia or indwelling IV catheters (endophthalmitis) (Chap. 34, p.269)
Fever, myalgias, and eruptive cutaneous nodules suggesting disseminated candidiasis (rash chapter, p.190)
Presence of an indwelling intravascular catheter or central line in a patient with candidemia (Chap. 34, p.269; Chap. 79)
harrison.prognosis: Mucocutaneous candidiasis is generally benign and responds to removal of predisposing factors plus topical or, when needed, systemic antifungal therapy. Systemic involvement is rare but life-threatening; candidemia and chronic disseminated candidiasis are serious complications in neutropenic and immunosuppressed patients (Chap. 60, p.432-433; Chap. 79, p.578).
pitfalls: Systemic therapy is usually reserved for immunosuppressed patients or those with chronic/recurrent disease who fail topical therapy, NOT routine mucocutaneous cases (Chap. 60, p.433).
Oral nystatin is effective ONLY for candidiasis of the gastrointestinal tract, not for systemic disease (Chap. 60, p.433).
Failure to remove predisposing factors (broad-spectrum antibiotics, chronic moisture/maceration) leads to treatment failure (Chap. 60, p.433).
In endogenous endophthalmitis, visual loss may sometimes be the ONLY symptom even without prominent ocular pain or injection (Chap. 34, p.269).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison frames candidiasis along a clinical spectrum rather than a formal grading scale: localized mucocutaneous disease (oral, esophageal, vulvovaginal, intertriginous, cutaneous) versus rare systemic/invasive disease (candidemia, chronic disseminated/hepatosplenic candidiasis). Invasive disease risk rises with prolonged profound neutropenia (ANC <500/uL) (Chap. 60, p.432-433; Chap. 79, p.578).
references: Harrison 22e p.578-621 (Chap. 79, infections in cancer patients)
Harrison 22e p.190 (nodular eruptions in immunocompromised hosts)
management: Treat localised mucocutaneous disease with a topical antifungal such as nystatin or clotrimazole
Use an oral azole such as fluconazole for oral, oesophageal or extensive mucosal candidiasis
Manage vulvovaginal candidiasis with a topical or single oral azole
Remove predisposing factors by optimising diabetic control, rationalising broad-spectrum antibiotics and improving denture hygiene and skin-fold dryness
Treat invasive disease and candidemia with a systemic antifungal such as an echinocandin and remove infected intravascular catheters
Perform dilated fundoscopy to detect candidal endophthalmitis when there is candidemia
